label: Guide for professionals
title: Becoming an autism assessor in the UK
metaTitle: How to become an autism assessor in the UK: tools, training and jobs | ND Resources
description: A UK guide to autism assessment for professionals: how NICE assessment pathways work for children and adults, the tools used (ADOS-2, ADI-R, DISCO and more), how assessors train, and how to find assessor jobs.
lede: How autism assessment works in the UK, the tools assessors use, how those skills are learnt, and how to find work as an assessor in the NHS or with private providers.
summary: In the UK, autism is diagnosed by registered clinicians (usually psychologists, psychiatrists or paediatricians), often working with speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and nurses in a multidisciplinary team.
Assessments follow NICE guidance: CG128 for children and young people, CG142 for adults. No single test or questionnaire can diagnose autism on its own.
The best-known tools are the ADOS-2 (an observation) and the ADI-R (a developmental interview). Clinical training in each takes 2 to 5 days and costs roughly £600 to £1,500 (November 2026).
Most assessors build experience in the NHS, then many also work for private or Right to Choose providers. Jobs are advertised on NHS Jobs, Trac, BPS Appointments and provider websites.

sections.heading: How autism assessment works in the UK
sections.html:
An autism assessment is a structured process that gathers information from several sources and then compares it with agreed diagnostic criteria. In the NHS in England, assessors are asked to describe autism using ICD-11 (the World Health Organization's classification), while the NHS still records diagnoses with ICD-10 codes. Many private services also refer to DSM-5-TR (the American classification). Both describe the same two areas: persistent differences in social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or sensory experience, present from early development.

The national guidance

  • NICE CG128 covers children and young people under 19 in England and Wales.
  • NICE CG142 covers adults.
  • NHS England's national framework for all-age autism assessment pathways and its operational guidance (2023) tell local NHS services how to organise assessment.
  • Scotland follows SIGN 145. Wales and Northern Ireland have their own service models built on similar principles.

Who carries out the assessment

For children, NICE CG128 recommends a local multidisciplinary autism team whose core members are a paediatrician and/or child and adolescent psychiatrist, a speech and language therapist, and a psychologist experienced with autistic children. The team should also have access to occupational therapy and other specialists.

For adults, NICE CG142 says assessment should be done by professionals who are trained and competent, and should be team-based and draw on a range of professions where possible.

NHS England's framework adds a useful distinction. A standard assessment can be done by one or more suitably qualified clinicians. An enhanced assessment involves two or more clinicians and uses validated tools, a clinical interview and observation. It defines a clinician as someone registered with the GMC, HCPC or NMC, and is clear that registration alone does not make someone competent to assess autism: specific training is needed too. Paediatricians, psychiatrists and clinical psychologists can usually cover every part of an assessment; speech and language therapists and occupational therapists usually contribute as part of a team.

What a full assessment includes

  • Concerns and context: what the person, family or referrer has noticed, and life at home, school or work.
  • Developmental history: usually a structured interview with a parent or someone who knew the person as a child.
  • Observation and interaction: time spent with the person, often using a structured observation such as the ADOS-2.
  • Health history and, for children, a physical examination.
  • Differential diagnosis: thinking about what else could explain the picture, such as language disorder, learning disability, trauma, attachment difficulties, anxiety or ADHD.
  • Co-occurring conditions: checking for ADHD, anxiety, sleep problems, epilepsy and others.
  • A profile of strengths and needs, not only a yes or no answer.
  • Feedback and a written report, shared sensitively, with a follow-up offered. CG128 suggests a follow-up within 6 weeks for children.

NICE says a child's assessment should start within 3 months of referral to the autism team. In practice, waits are often far longer: NHS England reported more than 125,000 people waiting for an autism assessment in mental health services in 2022, and numbers have grown since.

The single most important principle: diagnosis is a clinical judgement made from all the information together. NICE is explicit that no autism-specific tool should be relied on alone to diagnose autism, and screening questionnaires should never be used to make or rule out a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Children and adults: what differs
sections.html:
Children and young people

  • Usually referred by a GP, health visitor, school or SENCO.
  • Parents' account of early development is central.
  • Information from nursery or school is usually requested.
  • Led by community paediatrics or CAMHS, depending on age and area.
  • Outcome feeds into school support and, where needed, an EHC needs assessment.

Adults

  • Often self-referred to a GP, who may use the AQ-10 screen. NICE CG142 suggests offering a full assessment when the score is above 6 or clinical judgement suggests autism.
  • Early history may be hard to get, so assessors rely more on the person's own account.
  • Many adults, especially women and people who mask, have learned to hide their differences, so observation alone can miss autism.
  • Mental health history matters: autism is often missed or mislabelled as anxiety, depression or a personality disorder.
  • Run by adult autism or neurodevelopmental services.

sections.heading: The tools assessors use
sections.html:
Tools give structure and consistency. They do not make the diagnosis. Services choose tools to suit the person's age, language and needs. The table below covers the ones you will see most in UK job adverts and reports.

ToolWhat it isUsed with
ADOS-2Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule. A semi-structured, play- or conversation-based observation lasting about 40 to 60 minutes, coded against set behaviours. Five modules chosen by age and spoken language (Toddler, then 1 to 4).12 months to adulthood
ADI-RAutism Diagnostic Interview, Revised. A long structured interview with a parent or carer about development and current behaviour. Often 1.5 to 3 hours.Mental age over 2; carer needed
DISCODiagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders, developed by Lorna Wing and Judith Gould. A detailed interview that also maps wider needs and strengths. Training is run by the National Autistic Society.All ages
3diDevelopmental, Dimensional and Diagnostic Interview. A computer-assisted parent interview, shorter than the ADI-R.Children and young people
MIGDAS-2Monteiro Interview Guidelines for Diagnosing the Autism Spectrum. A sensory-based, conversational interview designed to feel more natural and to bring out the person's own perspective.Children, young people and adults
BOSABrief Observation of Symptoms of Autism. A shorter observation developed from the ADOS-2 for situations where a full ADOS-2 is not possible, for example with masks or remote assessment.Children and adults
ASDI and AAAInterview schedules for autistic people without a learning disability. Both are named in NICE CG142 for adults.Adults
SRS-2, SCQ, CARS-2Rating scales and questionnaires completed by parents, teachers or clinicians. Useful for gathering information across settings. Not diagnostic on their own.Mostly children
AQ, AQ-10, RAADS-R, CAT-QSelf-report questionnaires. The AQ-10 is a quick screen; RAADS-R is longer; CAT-Q measures camouflaging (masking). Screening only.Adults and older teens
Cognitive and sensory measuresFor example WISC-V or WAIS-IV (cognitive ability), and the Sensory Profile or Sensory Processing Measure. Used to build a profile and check for learning disability.Varies

Under NICE CG142, the formal tools suggested for adults without a learning disability are the AAA, ADI-R, ADOS, ASDI and RAADS-R; for adults with a learning disability, the ADOS and ADI-R. Children's guidance (CG128) does not name tools, but says to consider an autism-specific tool for the developmental history and for observation.

As an example of real-world practice, the private provider Compass Psychology describes using the ADI-R and ADOS-2 with at least two clinicians per assessment, plus cognitive testing where needed, and questionnaires such as the SCQ and SRS-2.

Most of these tools are "restricted": publishers sell them only to qualified professionals. For example, Hogrefe lists the ADOS-2 kit at qualification Level 3 and about £2,499 plus VAT for a hand-scored kit (November 2026).

sections.heading: How assessors are trained
sections.html:
Becoming an autism assessor is usually a specialism you add to a registered profession, not a job you train for from scratch. There are three layers.

1. A registered profession

ProfessionRegulatorTypical role in assessment
Clinical or counselling psychologistHCPCCan lead and diagnose; often runs ADOS-2, ADI-R and cognitive testing.
Educational psychologistHCPCContributes, especially for school-age children; may diagnose within some teams.
Psychiatrist or paediatricianGMCCan lead and diagnose; covers medical history, examination and co-occurring conditions.
Speech and language therapistHCPCAssesses communication and language; often co-runs the ADOS-2 within a team.
Occupational therapistHCPCAssesses sensory processing, motor skills and daily living within a team.
Nurse (learning disability or mental health)NMCAutism practitioner roles: history-taking, observation, coordination within a team.
Assistant psychologistNot regulatedSupports qualified staff: questionnaires, scoring, report drafting, under supervision.

The clinical psychology route is a psychology degree accredited by the British Psychological Society (BPS), relevant experience (often as an assistant psychologist), then a three-year, NHS-funded Doctorate in Clinical Psychology. Speech and language therapists and occupational therapists qualify through approved degree or master's courses; the Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists and the Royal College of Occupational Therapists list routes.

2. Tool training

The main tools need formal training before use. Courses in the UK as listed in November 2026 (prices change, so always check):

CourseProviderLengthApprox. price
Introduction to ADOS-2 (Modules 1 to 4)Hogrefe2 days online plus coding a video afterwards£600 + VAT
ADOS-2 Clinical TrainingPearson Clinical2 days online plus about 10 hours self-study (includes Toddler Module)£600 to £720
ADOS-2 trainingCompass Psychology4 days online plus coding a video afterwards£1,095 + VAT
ADI-R trainingCompass Psychology3 days online£895 + VAT
ADOS-2 and ADI-R Clinical ComboHogrefe5 days online£1,495 + VAT
DISCO trainingNational Autistic SocietySee providerSee provider

Things to know before you book:

  • Who can attend: providers expect a relevant degree and existing experience of autism. Hogrefe notes that some professions (for example educational psychologists, OTs, SLTs and nurses) can attend but would not make the final diagnostic decision on their own.
  • Clinical vs research reliability: clinical courses certify you for clinical use in the UK. Research reliability is a separate, stricter process, usually needing around 80% agreement with expert coding. Compass Psychology sells practice reliability videos.
  • Courses fill quickly: several Hogrefe dates for late 2026 and early 2027 were already fully booked when we checked.
  • A certificate is a start, not the finish. Pearson states plainly that attending the course is not enough to use the ADOS-2 competently.

3. Supervised practice

NHS England's operational guidance expects clinicians to use standardised tools only after training and enough experience, with sign-off as competent and ongoing supervision. In practice, new assessors co-run assessments with experienced colleagues, take part in team diagnostic discussions, and have their reports reviewed before working more independently. Useful extra learning includes autism in girls and women, masking, autism with learning disability, differential diagnosis, and neuro-affirming feedback and report writing.

sections.heading: How to get a job as an autism assessor
sections.html:
Where assessors work

  • NHS services: community paediatrics, CAMHS, adult autism or neurodevelopmental services, and learning disability teams. Salaried, with training and supervision built in.
  • Private and Right to Choose providers: in England, people referred for an assessment have a legal right to choose any provider that holds a relevant NHS contract, so many independent providers now carry out NHS-funded assessments (see an example NHS explanation and the Ombudsman's 2025 report). Roles are often sessional, part-time or remote.
  • Independent practice: experienced, registered clinicians run their own private assessment services. You will need your own insurance, tools, supervision and, depending on services offered, CQC registration.
  • Education and local authorities: educational psychology services contribute to assessments and to EHC needs assessments.

Typical NHS roles and pay

NHS roles are paid on Agenda for Change bands. Bands vary by trust and job, so treat these as a guide.

RoleTypical band2025/26 pay range (England)
Assistant psychologistBand 4 to 5£27,485 to £37,796
Autism practitioner (SLT, OT or nurse)Band 6 to 7£38,682 to £54,710
Clinical psychologist (newly qualified)Band 7£47,810 to £54,710
Senior or lead clinical psychologistBand 8a to 8b£55,690 to £74,896
Consultant psychologist or service leadBand 8c and abovefrom £76,965
Psychiatrists and paediatriciansMedical pay scalesSee NHS Employers

Pay ranges are the 2025/26 Agenda for Change rates published by NHS Employers, before any London or high-cost area supplement. They are approximate and may have changed since. Private providers often pay per assessment or per session; rates vary widely, so ask during recruitment.

Where jobs are advertised

  • NHS Jobs and Trac: search "autism assessment", "neurodevelopmental", "ASD pathway" or "ADOS".
  • BPS Appointments for psychology roles; RCSLT and RCOT job boards for therapists.
  • Careers pages of Right to Choose and private providers, and general boards such as LinkedIn and Indeed.
  • Word of mouth: many sessional roles are filled through ADOS-2 course contacts, supervision networks and professional groups.

A practical route in

  1. Get registered in a relevant profession (HCPC, GMC or NMC).
  2. Build autism experience in a team that assesses or supports autistic people, for example CAMHS, learning disability or a specialist school.
  3. Ask to shadow assessments and join diagnostic team meetings.
  4. Do ADOS-2 training, then ADI-R or another developmental interview. Many NHS teams will fund this once you are in post.
  5. Co-run assessments under supervision and keep a log of cases, ages and tools used.
  6. Apply for assessor roles, highlighting your tool training, supervised cases, report writing and understanding of NICE guidance and neuro-affirming practice.

label: Guide for professionals
title: Becoming an ADHD assessor in the UK
metaTitle: How to become an ADHD assessor in the UK: NHS and private practice | ND Resources
description: A UK guide for professionals on becoming an ADHD assessor: NICE NG87 assessment, the tools used (DIVA-5, ACE+, Conners 4, QbTest), training and prescribing, and NHS vs private practice jobs compared.
lede: How ADHD assessment works in the UK, the tools assessors use, how the skills are learnt, and how working in the NHS compares with private practice.
summary: ADHD is diagnosed by psychiatrists and paediatricians, and increasingly by trained specialist nurses and psychologists working in teams. Only prescribers can start medication.
Assessment follows NICE NG87: a full clinical interview, history from childhood, reports from others, and evidence of impairment in more than one setting. A questionnaire alone is never enough.
Common tools are the DIVA-5, ACE+, Conners 4, CAARS-2 and, for ages 6 to 17, QbTest.
NHS roles are salaried (about £38,700 to £62,700 for Band 6 to 8a in 2025/26); private and Right to Choose work is more flexible but brings extra rules on regulation and prescribing.

sections.heading: How ADHD assessment works in the UK
sections.html:
ADHD is diagnosed through a clinical assessment that looks at a person's attention, activity and impulsivity across their life and in different settings. In the UK, diagnosis follows NICE NG87 (Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management), which covers children, young people and adults. Clinicians use the DSM-5-TR criteria for ADHD or the ICD-11 criteria (6A05).

Who can diagnose

NICE says a diagnosis should only be made by a specialist psychiatrist, a paediatrician, or another appropriately qualified healthcare professional with training and expertise in diagnosing ADHD. In practice that means:

  • Children: community paediatricians and child and adolescent psychiatrists, often with specialist ADHD nurses and psychologists in the team.
  • Adults: psychiatrists in adult ADHD or neurodevelopmental services, increasingly supported by specialist nurses, nurse prescribers, pharmacists and psychologists.
  • Psychologists often carry out the diagnostic assessment, especially in multidisciplinary and private services, but cannot prescribe. If medication is wanted, a prescriber reviews the case.

What a full assessment includes

  • A clinical interview about symptoms now and in childhood, often using a structured interview such as the DIVA-5 or ACE+.
  • Developmental and psychiatric history.
  • Reports from others: parents, partners, teachers or school reports, to show symptoms in more than one setting.
  • Impairment: NICE asks for symptoms that cause at least moderate psychological, social, educational or occupational impairment.
  • Mental state and physical health, including blood pressure, heart rate, weight and heart history if medication may follow.
  • Differential diagnosis and co-occurring conditions: anxiety, depression, trauma, sleep problems, bipolar disorder, substance use, learning difficulties and autism.
  • Feedback and a written report with recommendations for treatment, school or workplace adjustments.

As with autism, rating scales and questionnaires are aids, not answers. NICE is clear that ADHD should not be diagnosed from a rating scale or observation alone.

Why assessors are in demand

NHS England's independent ADHD Taskforce (final report November 2025) found that NHS services cannot currently meet demand. It reported waits of more than 2 years in many places, and 10 to 15 years in some areas. It recommended treating ADHD more like other common long-term conditions, sharing work between specialists, GPs and nurses, setting out what counts as an ADHD-qualified professional, and bringing all NHS and private ADHD providers under CQC oversight. Expect the rules on who can assess to become clearer and stricter over the next few years.

sections.heading: Children and adults: what differs
sections.html:
Children and young people

  • Referred by a GP, school, SENCO or health visitor.
  • Usually led by community paediatrics or CAMHS.
  • Parent and teacher rating scales (such as the Conners 4) are standard.
  • NICE recommends QbTest as an option for ages 6 to 17, alongside a full clinical assessment.
  • Parent training and school support come before or alongside medication for younger children.

Adults

  • Referred by a GP, often after a screening questionnaire such as the ASRS.
  • Led by adult ADHD or neurodevelopmental services, usually within mental health trusts.
  • Childhood history comes from the person, family and old school reports where available.
  • Many adults, especially women, were missed as children and have learned to compensate.
  • Medication is usually started by the specialist, then handed to the GP under a shared care agreement.

sections.heading: The tools assessors use
sections.html:
These are the tools most often named in UK reports and job adverts. Most are aids to a clinical interview, not tests that give a yes or no.

ToolWhat it isUsed with
DIVA-5Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in adults. A semi-structured interview based on DSM-5 that goes through each symptom in adulthood and childhood, with examples. Widely used in the NHS and private services. Downloaded per use (about €10 each, November 2026) from the DIVA Foundation. Young DIVA-5 covers ages 5 to 17 and DIVA-5 ID covers people with intellectual disability.Adults; versions for children
ACE and ACE+ADHD Child Evaluation (ACE) and its adult version (ACE+), semi-structured interviews developed by Professor Susan Young, freely available to clinicians.Children (ACE) and adults (ACE+)
ASRS v1.1Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale from the World Health Organization. Its 6-question Part A is a common GP screen.Adults
Conners 4 and CAARS-2Rating scales completed by the person, parents, teachers or a partner. Conners 4 covers ages 6 to 18; CAARS-2 covers adults. Sold to qualified professionals.Children and adults
SNAP-IV, VanderbiltShorter parent and teacher rating scales, often used for screening and monitoring.Children
QbTestA computer test that measures attention, impulsivity and movement. NICE recommends it as an option for ages 6 to 17, alongside a standard clinical assessment. For adults, NICE says it should be used only in research for now.6 to 17 (NHS use)
WFIRS, BRIEF-2Questionnaires on day-to-day impairment (WFIRS) and executive function (BRIEF-2).Children and adults
Cognitive testsFor example WISC-V or WAIS-IV, used where learning difficulties or a fuller profile need checking.Varies

For example, Compass Psychology describes using the DIVA-5 or Young DIVA-5, with at least two clinicians per assessment and optional cognitive testing.

sections.heading: How ADHD assessors are trained
sections.html:
1. A registered profession

ProfessionRegulatorCan diagnose?Can prescribe?
Psychiatrist (child or adult)GMCYesYes
PaediatricianGMCYes (children)Yes
GP with a special interestGMCIn some local schemes, with extra trainingUsually continues medication under shared care
Specialist ADHD nurseNMCIn many services, within a team and with trainingYes, if a qualified independent prescriber (V300)
Pharmacist prescriberGPhCNot usuallyYes, if an independent prescriber; mainly titration and reviews
Clinical or counselling psychologistHCPCYes in many services, within a teamNo
Occupational therapist or SLTHCPCContributes within a teamNo
Assistant psychologistNot regulatedNo; gathers information under supervisionNo

2. ADHD training

There is no single licence to assess ADHD. Employers look for recognised training, supervised practice and, for prescribers, an independent prescribing qualification. Courses listed in November 2026 (prices change, so always check):

CourseProviderLengthApprox. price
Adult ADHD Foundation CourseRoyal College of PsychiatristsAbout 10 hours online (e-learning plus a live day)£84 to £238 depending on membership
Adult ADHD diagnostic assessment and treatmentSouth London and Maudsley (Estia Centre)2 days online plus optional case discussions£1,078 (external)
Diagnosis and assessment of adults with ADHDUKAAN (via King's College London)See providerSee provider
DIVA-5 training videosDIVA FoundationOnline video seriesSee provider
Non-medical independent prescribing (V300)Universities approved by the NMC, GPhC or HCPCAbout 6 months part-timeOften funded by NHS employers
  • A certificate is not competence. The South London and Maudsley course says plainly that finishing it does not qualify anyone to practise independently as an ADHD assessor.
  • Know your limits: NICE expects people starting medication to have training and expertise in diagnosing and managing ADHD.
  • Watch for new standards: the ADHD Taskforce asked NHS England and the Department of Health and Social Care to define what an ADHD-qualified professional is.

3. Supervised practice

New assessors usually observe experienced colleagues, then run assessments with a senior clinician reviewing their reports and diagnostic decisions. Prescribers also learn titration, physical health monitoring and shared care before working independently.

sections.heading: NHS or private practice: jobs compared
sections.html:
Most ADHD assessors work in the NHS, in private practice, or both. This table sets out the main differences.

NHSPrivate practice and Right to Choose
Where you workCommunity paediatrics, CAMHS, adult ADHD or neurodevelopmental services in mental health trusts, and some GP-led local schemes.Private clinics, online providers, and independent providers holding NHS Right to Choose contracts. Some clinicians set up their own practice.
Who paysNHS-funded; free for patients.Patients pay privately, or the NHS pays through Right to Choose (England only).
EmploymentSalaried, Agenda for Change or medical pay scales, with pension, training and supervision.Employed, sessional or self-employed. Often paid per assessment or per session; rates vary, so ask.
Typical pay or fees2025/26 Agenda for Change: Band 6 £38,682 to £46,580; Band 7 £47,810 to £54,710; Band 8a £55,690 to £62,682.Fees to patients vary widely between providers. For example, Compass Psychology lists ADHD assessments from £1,895 (November 2026).
RegulationTrust governance, NHS clinical supervision and CQC-registered trusts.You must be registered (GMC, NMC, HCPC or GPhC), insured, and usually work for or register a CQC-registered service. Private prescribing of stimulants needs a private controlled drugs prescriber code and FP10PCD forms.
MedicationSpecialist starts and adjusts medication, then hands over to the GP under a shared care agreement.GPs can decline shared care with private providers, so patients may have to keep paying for prescriptions. Right to Choose providers usually follow NHS shared care rules.
ProsStable job, team support, training budgets, complex cases.Flexible hours, remote work, often higher earnings per assessment.
Watch out forLong waiting lists and heavy caseloads.Quality concerns in parts of the sector; the Taskforce wants all providers held to the same standards.

Typical NHS ADHD roles

RoleTypical band2025/26 pay range (England)
ADHD practitioner or assistant psychologistBand 4 to 5£27,485 to £37,796
Specialist ADHD nurseBand 6 to 7£38,682 to £54,710
ADHD nurse or pharmacist prescriber, clinical psychologistBand 7 to 8a£47,810 to £62,682
Lead nurse, senior psychologist or service leadBand 8a to 8c£55,690 to £88,682
Specialty doctor or consultant psychiatrist or paediatricianMedical pay scalesSee NHS Employers

Pay ranges are the 2025/26 Agenda for Change rates from NHS Employers, before London or high-cost area supplements. Bands vary by trust. Treat all figures as approximate and check current rates.

Where jobs are advertised

  • NHS Jobs and Trac: search "ADHD", "neurodevelopmental", "ADHD nurse" or "ADHD prescriber".
  • BPS Appointments, RCPsych and BMJ Careers for psychologists and doctors; nursing job boards for nurses.
  • Careers pages of private and Right to Choose providers, LinkedIn and Indeed.

A practical route in

  1. Get registered as a doctor, nurse, pharmacist or psychologist.
  2. Work in mental health, CAMHS or paediatrics to build experience with ADHD and the conditions it is often mixed up with.
  3. Shadow ADHD clinics and learn the DIVA-5 or ACE+ and the main rating scales.
  4. Take a recognised course, such as the RCPsych foundation course or an NHS trust programme.
  5. If you are a nurse or pharmacist, add independent prescribing (V300): prescribers are in particular demand.
  6. Assess under supervision and keep a log of cases, ages and outcomes.
  7. Then apply for NHS ADHD posts or sessional private work, or, once experienced, set up your own practice with the right insurance and CQC registration.
